title: Offering it up (Colossians 1:24)
hook: Catholics can unite suffering to Christ's for others
tomorrow: a long sadness: a spiritual test, or an illness?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: carried together, four friends and a hole in the roof. Today, a stranger kind of carrying.

Stub your toe in some Catholic homes and you'll hear it before the pain fades: offer it up. It can sound like a polite way to say stop complaining. But it comes from a verse that, read cold, sounds almost wrong. Paul, writing to the Colossians in chains, says he fills up what is wanting of the sufferings of Christ. Wanting? After the cross, what could possibly be missing?

Here's the whole line, in the Douay-Rheims: "Who now rejoice in my sufferings for you, and fill up those things that are wanting of the sufferings of Christ, in my flesh, for his body, which is the church." Catholics answer the puzzle this way. Nothing is missing from what Christ did; his sacrifice is enough for the whole world. What's left open is room for us. Saint John Paul the Second wrote a letter, On the Christian Meaning of Human Suffering, that dwells on this verse. He said the redemption is complete and yet stays open to every human suffering joined to it. Christ lets his body, the Church, share in his work, for one another. That's redemptive suffering. Notice the last words: for his body. Paul's pain is aimed at someone. Some Christian readers hear the verse differently, as Paul's hardships for the gospel, and the Church doesn't ask anyone to go looking for pain. One to tell a friend: offering it up doesn't mean pretending it doesn't hurt. You can still take the medicine, see the doctor, and say out loud that it's hard. You offer the part you can't change, and you name who it's for.
screen: `FILL UP WHAT IS WANTING.` · `NOTHING MISSING; ROOM LEFT OPEN.` · `FOR HIS BODY, WHICH IS THE CHURCH.` · `NOT PRETENDING IT DOESN'T HURT.` · then, large: `OFFERED FOR SOMEONE.`

segments.voice: Notice one small discomfort you already have: a tired back, a sore knee, a knot of worry. Don't fix it for these two minutes. Say out loud the name of one person you'd offer it for, and keep them in mind until the bell. If you pray, you can offer it for them in your own words.
Redemptive suffering. Pain joined to Christ's and offered for others, the Catholic meaning of offer it up. Today's word.
The line to keep: offered for someone, with a real name attached to it. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics speak of 'offering it up': uniting a pain or hardship to Christ's suffering for someone else's good; some begin the day with a Morning Offering of its joys and sufferings.

fork.setup: your friend is stuck on a long bus ride to an away game, carsick and miserable. she says, 'offering it up, I guess.' what's the best way to help her mean it?

tell her it only counts if she doesn't complain at all.

fork.reveal: offering it up isn't faking fine or chasing pain. it's naming someone and joining what you can't change to Christ's, for them.
